p: In the annalistic tradition a plebeian named Hortensius was appointed dictator around 287 BCE to deal with a civil uprising, which led to the secession of the plebs to the Janiculum hill; they returned only after the law had been passed in the Centuriate Assembly. The annals put the uprising down to debt, with a call to arms against the Lucanians as the immediate occasion, since the patricians needed plebeian manpower for the war.

There is considerable reason to doubt this account, which Livy attributes to an urban rabble in the forum. Large masses of urban poor did not really exist in the middle Republic, and rural landowners controlled 29 of the voting blocs of the Plebeian Council, which never numbered more than 35. The more likely cause is the wish of rural plebeians to control the distribution of the public lands won in the Third Samnite War, though the extreme measures of the consuls suggest considerable unrest in the city as well. An organised movement was needed to pass such a law, and it was probably coordinated by the plebeian tribunes.

In the early Republic the resolutions of the Plebeian Council, the plebiscita, bound only plebeians, because only plebeians voted there. The lex Valeria-Horatia of 449 BCE allowed them to bind all Romans if the Senate ratified them, and the lex Publilia of 339 BCE moved the Senate's approval to before the vote. The Hortensian law removed the requirement altogether. A plebiscitum remained distinct in name from a lex but was now treated as if it were one; later all binding laws came to be called leges.

The law also restricted when votes could be held. They were no longer allowed on market days, when they could have interfered with business, which hindered rural plebeians from taking part, since those were the days when they would have been in the city.

The law secured theoretically equal political rights for patricians and plebeians. It established the pre-eminence of the Tribal Assembly and the Plebeian Council in legislation, so that in the late Republic the other assemblies passed mainly minor and procedural laws, and it made the plebeians and their tribunes important political players, which the earlier laws had failed to do.

notes: The article spells the 339 law both 'lex Publilia' and 'lex Pubilia'; I used Publilia.

'so that in the late Republic the other assemblies passed mainly minor and procedural laws' is my reading of an ambiguous sentence ('It also cemented the pre-eminence of the Tribal Assembly and the Plebeian Council in legislation, with primarily minor and procedural laws passed in the late Republic'). Cut the clause if in doubt.
The article's first name for the dictator, Quintus, is in the existing description; the Causes section says only 'a plebeian dictator by the name of Hortensius'.
